questions.question: Describe the gold-foil experiment and its conclusion, then give the charges, relative masses and locations of the three subatomic particles, including what the notation aluminium-27 unpacks into.
questions.expected_answer: Alpha particles were fired at very thin gold foil. Nearly all passed straight through, showing atoms are mostly empty space, but a tiny fraction bounced almost straight back — only possible if nearly all the atom's mass and all its positive charge are concentrated in a minute central nucleus. The particles: the proton, charge plus one, relative mass one, in the nucleus; the neutron, no charge, relative mass one, also in the nucleus; the electron, charge minus one, mass about one two-thousandth of a proton's — ignored in mass totals — occupying the space around the nucleus and doing all the chemistry. In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons. Aluminium twenty-seven, written with mass number 27 as a superscript and atomic number 13 as a subscript to the left of Al, unpacks as 13 protons, 27 minus 13 equals 14 neutrons, and 13 electrons when neutral.

questions.question: Define isotopes, explain why they are chemically identical, and calculate boron's relative atomic mass from 20 percent boron-10 and 80 percent boron-11, explaining what the answer's position reveals.
questions.expected_answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element — the same atomic number and proton count — with different numbers of neutrons and therefore different mass numbers: boron-10 holds 5 protons and 5 neutrons, boron-11 holds 5 protons and 6 neutrons. Because chemical behaviour is run entirely by the electrons, and isotopes carry identical electron arrangements, they are chemically identical and differ only in mass. The periodic table prints the relative atomic mass: the weighted average of the isotope masses by natural abundance — not a halfway point, since the more common isotope counts for more. For boron: 20 over 100 times 10 gives 2, plus 80 over 100 times 11 gives 8,8, summing to 10,8. No single atom weighs 10,8; the family averages it. The answer sitting far closer to 11 than to 10 announces that the heavier isotope dominates four to one — and reading chlorine's 35,5, which sits close to 35, the same way reveals that there the lighter isotope dominates.

questions.question: State the three filling rules for electrons, write the sp notation for aluminium, potassium and calcium, and explain the 4s quirk and the self-check.
questions.expected_answer: Electrons occupy energy levels containing orbitals — an s orbital per level holding up to two electrons, and sets of three p orbitals from level 2 upward holding up to six — with every orbital sleeping at most two electrons. Rule one, the Aufbau principle: fill from the lowest energy upward, in the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s. Rule two: at most two electrons per orbital, and a pair must have opposite spins, drawn as up and down arrows. Rule three, Hund's rule: across equal-energy p orbitals, electrons occupy empty orbitals singly before any pairing — phosphorus places one electron in each 3p orbital. The 4s quirk: 4s is slightly lower in energy than 3d, so it fills before 3d, which is why the order ends at 4s for elements up to Z equals 20. Configurations: aluminium, 13 electrons — 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p1; potassium, 19 — 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1; calcium, 20 — the same closing 4s2. The self-check: the superscripts must sum back to the atomic number, and the outermost — valence — electrons are the ones the periodic table and bonding topics count.
